terms.meaning: The basic unit of life. All living things are made of cells.
The thin outer boundary of the cell, which controls what goes in and out.
The jelly-like material that fills the cell around the nucleus.
The part that controls the cell’s activities and holds the genetic material.
A rigid extra covering around the membrane in plants, fungi and bacteria.
The region in a bacterium that holds its genetic material, with no nuclear membrane around it.
A tiny agent that reproduces only inside the cells of a host.

items.name: Who named the cell?
items.formula: Robert Hooke, looking at thin slices of cork in 1665.
items.example: He saw small compartments like a honeycomb.

items.name: Father of microbiology
items.formula: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who built better microscopes to see living microbes.
items.example: He looked at tiny life in pond water.

items.name: Plant cell and animal cell
items.formula: Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
items.example: An onion peel cell has a wall. A cheek cell does not.

items.name: Stains for slides
items.formula: Onion peel: safranin. Cheek cells: methylene blue. Glycerin stops drying.
items.example: Staining makes the parts easier to see.

items.name: Shape fits the job
items.formula: Muscle cells are spindle-shaped. Nerve cells are long and branched.
items.example: A long nerve cell carries messages across the body.

items.name: Levels of organisation
items.formula: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism
items.example: Muscle cells form muscle tissue, which forms part of the heart.

items.name: Largest single cell
items.formula: The ostrich egg yolk, about 130 to 170 mm across.
items.example: Most cells can be seen only through a microscope.

items.name: Single-celled microbes
items.formula: Bacteria, protozoa such as Amoeba, yeast, and some algae.

items.name: Many-celled microbes
items.example: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, but a mould has many cells.

items.name: Yeast
items.formula: Respires on sugar and gives off carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise.
items.example: Bread and idli batter are soft because of these gas bubbles.

items.name: Lactobacillus
items.formula: Turns milk sugar into lactic acid, setting milk into curd.
items.example: Lukewarm milk with a little curd sets by morning.

items.name: Rhizobium
items.formula: Lives in the root nodules of pulses and fixes nitrogen from the air.
items.example: Farmers grow pulses to improve the soil.

items.name: Biogas
items.formula: Bacteria break down waste without oxygen, giving methane and carbon dioxide.
items.example: Biogas from dung can be used as cooking fuel.

items.name: Compost
items.formula: Bacteria and fungi break dead plants and peels into rich manure.
items.example: Kitchen peels become compost in a pit.

items.name: Oil-eating bacteria
items.formula: Dr Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty developed a bacterium that breaks down crude oil.
items.example: It can help to clean up oil spills.

items.name: Microalgae
items.formula: They photosynthesise and give more than half of the Earth’s oxygen.
items.example: Spirulina is also used as a food supplement.

mistakes.text: A cell wall is not only in plants. Fungi and bacteria have one too, and animal cells do not.
Bacteria do have genetic material, but no well-defined nucleus.
Viruses cannot reproduce on their own. They need a host cell.
Not all microbes are harmful. Many are needed for curd, compost and soil fertility.
